description: Hi, I’m Nima, a final-year engineering student from Thiruvananthapuram. I like building web apps and trying out AI, and I’m joining Space Apps to make something useful with real NASA data.
summary:
Fire behaves differently in microgravity, yet the experimental evidence that explains how is scattered across technical NASA reports and tables that are hard for non-specialists to compare. FlameLens is an interactive, AI-powered platform that makes this research accessible for the “Flame in Freefall” challenge. We transformed published observations from NASA’s Saffire-I, Saffire-II and BASS-II investigations into structured, traceable datasets, kept separate because their apparatus and conditions differ. Users can filter by material, oxygen and airflow, explore flame-spread behaviour through interactive visualizations, and ask natural-language questions answered by Claude strictly from the selected data.

FlameLens is distinctive for its scientific restraint: missing values are never replaced with zeros, derived oxygen estimates are labelled with their method and confidence rather than presented as NASA measurements, and rankings are disabled when data are insufficient. Its heuristic risk indicator is an exploration aid, not a validated prediction model, and AI explanations are not safety certifications. By turning dispersed experimental evidence into something people can explore and question, FlameLens supports clearer understanding of spacecraft fire behaviour as humanity prepares for longer missions beyond Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works
FlameLens is an interactive, AI-powered dashboard that turns published NASA microgravity combustion experiments into something anyone can explore. We extracted observations from Saffire-I/II (Ferkul et al., 2017: 11 observations, 4 with numerical spread rates) and the BASS-II Summary Report (Olson et al., 2021: 20 parent tests, 39 flow and flame-spread records) into structured, source-referenced datasets. Users choose a dataset, filter by material, oxygen, pressure and airflow, and explore flame spread through interactive charts. They can also use two AI features:

  • AI Insights, which writes plain-English summaries.
  • Ask the Data, which answers natural-language questions using only the currently selected data.

Benefits and intended impact
Fire behaves differently in microgravity, but the evidence is scattered across technical reports and tables. FlameLens makes it searchable, comparable and understandable for students, researchers and the public. It supports fire-safety awareness for future human space exploration. It is an exploration tool, not a certified safety system.

Tools and technologies

  • Python, Streamlit, Pandas and Plotly for the app, data processing and visualization.
  • Anthropic Claude API for explanations and question answering, with rule-based offline responses as a fallback.
  • NASA Technical Reports Server publications as data sources.
  • GitHub for version control.

What makes it creative and different

  • Scientific honesty is built in. Missing values stay empty rather than becoming zero. Saffire and BASS-II are kept separate because their apparatus differs.
  • Estimates are labelled as estimates. Four segment-level oxygen values were derived from the report’s stated linear-profile method and Figure 5.2. They are labelled by method and confidence (three medium, one low) and are never presented as NASA measurements. Initial and final oxygen are never silently substituted.
  • The app refuses unsupported analysis. Material rankings switch off when data are insufficient, and the AI is instructed to say when something is not in the dataset.

Factors our team considered

  • Data provenance: every record links to its source document.
  • Differences between experimental setups.
  • Limited numerical data, and the risk of the AI over-claiming.

We tested the AI with 15 predefined questions covering flame spread, oxygen, airflow, pressure, material comparisons and missing data, and checked the answers against the datasets. The heuristic risk indicator is not a validated fire-risk model. This project is independent and is not endorsed by NASA.
dataRefs: Saffire – Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests (2017)
BASS-II – Burning and Suppression of Solids-II Summary Report (2021)
